title: Physiological evaluation of Quarter Horses undergoing training focused on hippotherapy
author: Lara Carolynne
materials: wereentered based on information provided by the weather app (Apple Weather‱, iOS)on all days of the experiment to reduce environmental variables that couldinfluence the ocular temperature result. Surface emissivity was adjusted to Ɛ = 0.98 inall collections, following the appropriate value for mammalian skin [34]. The first collection began at 8:30 am inside the stable, sheltered from directlight, where baseline thermographic images were captured 0.5 m from the lefteye [35]. The images were evaluated immediately after capture to avoid errors and artifacts(blur, flies, dirt, closed eye), repeating the capture if necessary to ensurequality during analysis. On training days, the second collection took placeinside the round pen or arena, both covered. The collection and work sequencewas randomized by a draw, evaluating them on 2 consecutive mornings (fouranimals on the first day and three on the second day). The images were storedon a 128 GB SD memory card for later processing on a computer using IRISoftsoftware (PoliScan‱, FLIR Systems Inc., Wilsonville, OR, USA), selecting onlythe images that presented the best technical quality, with sharp focus, absenceof thermal artifacts, and the eye fully open. Plasmacortisol: Blood samples were obtained via jugular vein venipuncture to measureplasma cortisol levels [36]. The site was previously cleaned; the samples were collected using disposable needles (25.0 x 0.8 mm) and stored in 10-ml BD Vacutainer ‱ tubes(without anticoagulant) for storage and subsequent processing. They werecollected from 10 am onwards, considering the circadian rhythm of cortisol inhorses [37] and the maximum cortisol peak in the morning (between 6 and 8 am) [38] to standardize the tests and avoid alterations resulting from this factor. The collection and worksequence was randomized by a draw, evaluating them on two consecutive mornings(four animals on the first day and three on the second day). Each horse underwentcollections at two different times: first, pre-exercise samples (10 am) werecollected inside the stables (5 to 10 minutes between entering and leaving thestable), thus obtaining baseline plasma cortisol samples; then, samples werecollected in the round pen or arena (both covered), immediately aftercompleting the proposed exercises, to compare any changes resulting from thetraining. All samples were transported under refrigeration to the VeterinaryMultipurpose Laboratory of the University of Brasília (UnB, Brasília, Brazil),where they were stored. At this stage, the samples obtained in tubes withoutanticoagulant were centrifuged for 10 minutes (Kasvi ‱ , modelK14-4000, Brazil) at 4000 rpm for plasma separation. Then, the refrigerated plasmawas sent to the specialized Veterinary Endocrinology Laboratory BET Labs(Niterói, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil), to determine blood cortisol levels. Thetechnique used was solid-phase radioimmunoassay (RIA) with commercial kits(Siemens Healthcare Diagnostics Inc., Tarrytown, NY, USA). All tests wereperformed in duplicate. PTPHSteps:

steps.title: Animal Acclimation and Health Screening
steps.instruction: Conduct a 30-day adaptation period to familiarize animals with stalls, daily handling, and the hippotherapy center routine.

substeps.instruction: Perform clinical and laboratory examinations, preventive dental treatments, vaccination, and deworming.
Implement daily individual handling, hygiene, manipulation, halter training, and release into collective paddocks.
Ensure a single person performs daily handling under trainer supervision.

steps.title: Phase 1: Communication and Integration
steps.instruction: Execute groundwork in a round pen for 30 days (4 sessions/week, ~30 min/animal) to develop communication and body awareness without riding.

substeps.instruction: Lead the animal to the center of the round pen using a halter and long lead.
Stimulate circular movement (5 repetitions each side) using a stick moved posteriorly to the croup area (pressure and release) and hand signals.
Use a vocal command to stop and lead the animal back to the center.
Release the animal from the lead and perform circular movements and voluntary following at a walk using vocal commands.
Train walk, trot, and gallop both with a lead and at liberty.

steps.title: Phase 2: Desensitization
steps.instruction: Conduct desensitization for 30 days (3 sessions/week, ~30 min/animal) to reduce reactivity to stimuli.

substeps.instruction: Lead animal to round pen; allow a short period of free movement using Phase 1 commands before replacing the halter.
Apply tactile stimulation with a stick, then by hand, in the following sequence: head, neck, trunk, back, loin, rump, and limbs (bilaterally).
Introduce visual and auditory stimuli using a stick (movements around/above animal and ground vibrations) and a flag stick (approach and retreat movements).
Apply stimuli while the animal is static, then progress to walk, trot, and gallop.
Introduce the saddle and tighten the girth (using a girth and belly band) starting at the end of day 15.
Continue until the animal remains calm at a walk and trot in a circle on the lead with the saddle.

steps.title: Phase 3: Capacity Building and Skills Development
steps.instruction: Perform qualification training for 60 days (4 sessions/week, ~40 min/animal) using a 30 x 40 m covered arena with non-woven fabric and sand floor.

substeps.instruction: Introduce forward, sideways, circular, stopping, and backing movements, and adapt to riding equipment (complete bridle, blanket, complete saddle).

Implement a desensitization circuit with the following objects/stimuli: colored cards and Velcro (tactile/auditory), clipboard and sheets (dropped on ground), four large plastic hoops (walk through), exercise ball (spontaneous interaction), unknown people (gentle touch, intense touch, verbal interaction, sudden high-pitched vocal stimulus), soccer ball (rolling along body), miniature saddle with figures, full-length mirror, four colored rings (placed on ears), and a plastic hula hoop (around neck).
Apply auditory stimuli via speaker: numerical counting (1-5), names of days of the week, and a recording of a child screaming.
Simulate a final hippotherapy session: saddle and warm up (5 turns each side at walk/trot), then ride the horse through the obstacle circuit while led on the left by an assistant.

steps.title: Continuous Gymnastics Program
steps.instruction: Perform physical conditioning and functional gymnastics for 30 minutes on alternate days to the specific phase training throughout Phases 1, 2, and 3.

substeps.instruction: Execute work on lead or at liberty (Phases 1, 2, and first 30 days of Phase 3) and outdoor/track work.
Perform basic training movements: 20-15-10-8 m circles, half turns, reverse half turns, serpentine turns, gallop starts, backing up, and shoulder forward.
In the final month, include leg yield, transitions in different gaits (walk, trot, gallop), small jumps (60-80 cm), poles, and barrels.

steps.title: Heart Rate (HR) Monitoring
steps.instruction: Continuously monitor HR using a Polar H10 device (21g, 34x65x10 mm) with a CR2025 battery, recording data via PolarEquine program on a Samsung S7 tablet.

substeps.instruction: Measure baseline HR (HR 0) in the stable starting at 8 am before activities.
Record minimum (HR Min), average (HR Ave), maximum (HR Max), and final (HR Fin) HR during and immediately after training sessions.

steps.title: Ocular Infrared Thermography (IRT)
steps.instruction: Capture thermal images of the left eye's lacrimal caruncle using a FLIR E40 camera (160 x 120 pixels) at a standardized distance of 0.5 m and 90° to the sagittal plane.

substeps.instruction: Calibrate equipment and enter ambient temperature (21.7 ± 1.3 °C) and relative humidity (75.2 ± 10.4%).
Set surface emissivity to Ɛ = 0.98.
Capture baseline images at 8:30 am inside the stable, sheltered from direct light.
Capture post-exercise images in the covered round pen or arena immediately after sessions.
Process images using IRISoft software, selecting only those with sharp focus and the eye fully open.

steps.title: Plasma Cortisol Analysis
steps.instruction: Collect blood samples via jugular vein venipuncture using 25.0 x 0.8 mm disposable needles and 10-ml BD Vacutainer tubes (no anticoagulant).

substeps.instruction: Collect baseline samples in the stable at 10 am (within 5-10 minutes of entering/leaving).
Collect post-exercise samples in the covered round pen or arena immediately after training.
Transport samples under refrigeration to the laboratory.
Centrifuge samples for 10 minutes at 4000 rpm (Kasvi K14-4000) for plasma separation.
Determine cortisol levels using solid-phase radioimmunoassay (RIA) with commercial kits (Siemens Healthcare Diagnostics Inc.) in duplicate.
